Yours is one of one.

Twelve forms, eight surfaces and forty fine adjustments: more variations than there are stars in the observable universe.

Three ways to command the light.

Twist to dim

The signature. The shade itself is the dimmer: turn it, and the light moves from candle-low to full glow. The mechanism stays hidden in the base.

Click to switch

One decisive click on the cord. A ready-wired cord drops into the base. Nothing to wire.

Tap to switch

A touch of the base. Cordless and battery powered, with nothing on show.

From first sketch to evening glow.

  1. Design

    Start from a piece in the Collection and shape it with sliders. The designer warns you before anything would fail to print.

  2. Print

    Download the files with a print card made for your lamp: layers, walls, temperatures. Any 3D printer will do.

  3. Light it

    Fit a warm LED and its switch, then let the room go dark around it.

    How to print a lamp.

    A lamp shows every flaw once it is lit from inside: a seam, a streak, a string. These settings give clean prints that glow evenly. For the exact numbers for your lamp, open step 06 in the designer: it makes a print card for every part.

    1. Choose your plastic

    PlasticHow it glowsHeatGood for
    PLAWell, in white, natural and pale coloursSoftens around 55–60 °C. Keep to an LED of 6 W or less.Your first lamps. The easiest to print.
    PETGClearer and more even, especially translucent PETGHandles about 75 °CShades that glow, and lamps that stay on for hours
    Silk PLAShiny, with a soft sheen. Less light passes through.Like PLABases and caps, or a shade that should shimmer more than glow
    Marble, wood or stone fillBarely at allLike PLABases, with a glowing shade on top

    Colour matters more than anything else. White, natural, cream and pale amber glow; black and dark colours block the light whatever the setting. Use dark colours for the base and let the shade do the glowing.

    The same bulb behind five plastics. Pale colours glow; black blocks the light whatever the settings.

    2. Settings for each part

    PartLayer heightWallsInfillAlso
    Shade0.12 mm for fine ribs, 0.16 mm otherwiseEnough to fill the wall: 2 for a 0.8 mm wall0%Slow the outer wall to about 40 mm/s, hide the seam in a groove
    Base0.2 mm315%, gyroidNo supports needed
    Diffuser0.2 mm1, in spiral vase modeNone3 bottom layers
    Gears and turn ring0.12 mm440%Fine layers keep the teeth smooth

    Why 0% infill on a shade? The shade wall should be made only of outlines. If the slicer squeezes infill or gap fill between them, it shows up as dark streaks once the lamp is on. Make the wall a whole number of lines: 0.8 mm is two lines from a 0.4 mm nozzle.

    A slice through the shade wall, one bead per layer. Extra plastic between the outlines blocks light in some layers: that is the dark streak you see when the lamp is on.

    One rib, cut in half. The dashed line is the shape you designed; thinner layers follow it more closely.

    3. Temperatures

    PlasticNozzleBedCooling fan
    PLA200–215 °C55–65 °C100%
    PETG230–245 °C70–85 °C30–50%
    ABS or ASA240–260 °C90–110 °COff or low, in an enclosure

    These are starting points. Your filament's box or reel has its own range: when they disagree, trust the box.

    4. Same setting, different names

    Every slicer calls things something slightly different. Here is where to find each one.

    SettingBambu Studio and OrcaSlicerPrusaSlicerCura
    WallsWall loopsPerimetersWall Line Count
    InfillSparse infill densityFill densityInfill Density
    SeamSeam positionSeam positionZ Seam Alignment
    Outer wall speedOuter wall (Speed tab)External perimeters (Speed)Outer Wall Speed
    Spiral vaseSpiral vaseSpiral vaseSpiralize Outer Contour
    BrimBrim typeBrim widthBuild Plate Adhesion Type

    5. When it goes wrong

    Measured from straight up. Past about 55° each layer hangs too far over the one below, and the plastic droops. The designer warns you in step 06.

    Each layer starts and ends at one point, and those points line up into a seam. On a ribbed shade, set the seam to Aligned or Sharpest corner and it tucks into a groove.

    • Dark streaks or blotches when the lamp is onSomething is filling the inside of the wall. Set infill to 0%, and match the wall count to the wall thickness (2 walls for 0.8 mm with a 0.4 mm nozzle).
    • A line running up one sideThat is the seam, where each layer starts. Set it to Aligned or Sharpest corner so it hides in a groove, or to Back and turn that side to the wall.
    • Hairs and strings inside the shadeUsually damp filament, especially PETG. Dry it, lower the nozzle by 5 °C, and check retraction is on.
    • Drooping, rough patches where the shade leans outThe wall leans too far to print in mid-air. Turn the cooling fan up and slow down, turn on supports, or reshape the shade in the designer. Step 06 warns you about this before you print.
    • The base lifts off the bed at the edgesClean the bed, add a 5 mm brim, and raise the bed temperature a little. ABS and ASA need an enclosure.
    • Gaps or holes in a thin wallThe wall is too thin for your nozzle, or the plastic is not flowing well. The designer warns when a wall is thinner than two lines. Print slower, and dry the filament.
    • Fine ribs come out soft and blurryUse thinner layers (0.12 mm) and a slower outer wall. Very shallow ribs need a 0.4 mm nozzle or smaller.

    6. Before you press print

    1. Import the 3MF or STL files at 100%. To make a lamp smaller, change it in the designer so the wall stays printable.
    2. Leave each part the way it comes in: the files already sit the right way up.
    3. Not sure? Print a test first: set the print scale in step 06 to about 30% for a quick model.
    4. Clean the bed and watch the first layer go down.
    5. Dry your PETG if it has been out of its bag for a while.

    Every lamp in the designer comes with its own print card: layer height, walls, temperatures and more, worked out for its exact shape. It is in step 06, and you can download it with the print files.

      Basic shape

      Cut-outs are holes through the shade. Their top edges print as short bridges, so keep them small for a clean result.

      Skin is a fine texture on the outside of the shade. It makes a much denser model, so files are larger.

      Socket hole sizes are typical values. Measure your own lamp holder before printing. Use LED bulbs only: printed plastic softens with heat.
